title: Explain Spark's unified memory model — executor memory is split into Execution Memory (shuffles, joins, sorts, aggregations) and Storage Memory (cached/persisted data), with a dynamic boundary between them (`spark.memory.fraction`, `spark.memory.storageFraction`) — and what happens when one side needs more (borrows from the other, evicts if necessary)?

s1_definition.profdef: Spark's unified memory model divides the fraction of executor heap it manages for data processing into two cooperating regions: Execution Memory, used for the working data of shuffles, joins, sorts, and aggregations, and Storage Memory, used to hold cached and persisted partitions. The split is governed by `spark.memory.fraction`, which sets how much of the usable heap the unified region occupies, and `spark.memory.storageFraction`, which sets the baseline share reserved for storage. The boundary is dynamic: if one region is idle, the other can borrow its space, but execution has priority — it can evict borrowed storage blocks when it needs the space back, whereas storage cannot forcibly reclaim memory that execution is actively using.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India imagine one large back room shared by two teams: the processing team (execution) doing the heavy work of sorting and matching slips, and the filing team (storage) keeping frequently-used ledgers handy on shelves. There is a soft line down the middle, but it moves: if the filing team has spare shelf space, the processing team can spread their work onto it, and vice versa. The rule is that processing work has priority — when the processing team suddenly needs the shelves back for an urgent sort, the filing team's borrowed ledgers get cleared off, because losing a cached ledger only means fetching it again, while interrupting an active sort would fail the job.
s1_definition.oneliner: Execution and Storage share one unified region with a movable boundary; either can borrow the other's idle space, but execution has priority and can evict borrowed cached blocks, while active execution memory is never evicted.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark's unified memory model divides the fraction of executor heap it manages for data processing into two cooperating regions: Execution Memory, used for the working data of shuffles, joins, sorts, and aggregations, and Storage Memory, used to hold cached and persisted partitions. The split is governed by `spark.memory.fraction`, which sets how much of the usable heap the unified region occupies, and `spark.memory.storageFraction`, which sets the baseline share reserved for storage. The boundary is dynamic: if one region is idle, the other can borrow its space, but execution has priority — it can evict borrowed storage blocks when it needs the space back, whereas storage cannot forcibly reclaim memory that execution is actively using.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India imagine one large back room shared by two teams: the processing team (execution) doing the heavy work of sorting and matching slips, and the filing team (storage) keeping frequently-used ledgers handy on shelves. There is a soft line down the middle, but it moves: if the filing team has spare shelf space, the processing team can spread their work onto it, and vice versa. The rule is that processing work has priority — when the processing team suddenly needs the shelves back for an urgent sort, the filing team's borrowed ledgers get cleared off, because losing a cached ledger only means fetching it again, while interrupting an active sort would fail the job.

**One line to remember:** Execution and Storage share one unified region with a movable boundary; either can borrow the other's idle space, but execution has priority and can evict borrowed cached blocks, while active execution memory is never evicted.

sections.s2_technical:
The executor heap is layered. A portion is reserved for Spark's internal objects (reserved memory). Of the remainder, `spark.memory.fraction`, defaulting to about 0.6, defines the unified region that Spark manages for both execution and storage; the rest is user memory for your own data structures and non-Spark objects. Keeping that 40 percent aside prevents user allocations from starving Spark's managed region.

Inside the unified region, `spark.memory.storageFraction`, defaulting to 0.5, sets the baseline fraction reserved for storage below which storage blocks are protected from eviction. This is not a hard wall — it is the point past which storage can be pushed back by execution. Above that protected baseline, the boundary floats according to demand.

Execution memory holds the transient working set of wide operations: the buffers for a shuffle write and read, the hash tables for a hash join or hash aggregation, and the sort buffers for a sort-merge join or an order-by. This memory is in active use during a task and cannot be evicted, because evicting it would corrupt the computation. If execution cannot get enough memory even after reclaiming from storage, it spills to disk.

Storage memory holds cached and persisted partitions from cache or persist. These blocks are evictable: if execution needs space and storage has borrowed beyond its protected baseline, Spark evicts cached blocks to free room. Eviction is cheap in correctness terms because an evicted cached partition can be recomputed from lineage or re-read, it just costs performance. This asymmetry — execution evicts storage but not vice versa — is the heart of the unified model.

The dynamic borrowing works both ways. If a query does no caching, storage memory sits idle and execution can use the whole unified region for its shuffles and joins, which is why heavy ETL with no caching still gets plenty of working memory. Conversely, if a query caches a large dataset and does little shuffling, storage can expand into execution's idle space. A senior-level nuance is that this unified design replaced the old static split where execution and storage had fixed, non-overlapping pools that frequently left one starved while the other was idle. The practical consequences today are that over-caching steals memory that joins and aggregations need, causing spills, and that the symptom of too much caching is not a cache error but slow shuffles — so when diagnosing memory pressure you look at the Spark UI storage tab and the spill metrics together, and you unpersist aggressively and avoid caching data used only once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a job that caches a reference dataset (accounts) and also performs a heavy shuffle join of transactions. Execution and storage must share memory sensibly so neither starves the other. This is the unified region with a dynamic boundary.

Problem 2 — A different job caches far too much and then runs a large aggregation; execution needs memory back and evicts borrowed cached blocks. This is execution's priority and storage eviction.

Problem 3 — A pure ETL job does no caching, so all unified memory is available to its shuffle. This is storage's idle space being borrowed by execution.

The demo models a unified memory region with configurable fractions, lets execution and storage request memory, and logs borrowing and eviction so the asymmetry is visible — execution reclaiming from storage but never the reverse.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a unified region of one thousand megabytes with a storage baseline of five hundred megabytes, and a sequence of memory requests.

Step 1: Storage requests seven hundred megabytes to cache the accounts dataset. There is one thousand free, so it succeeds, and storage now holds seven hundred — two hundred above its protected baseline of five hundred.

Step 2: Execution requests six hundred megabytes for the transactions join. Only three hundred is free, so execution evicts two hundred of the borrowed cached storage to bring storage back to its baseline of five hundred, freeing enough to grant the request. This shows execution's priority.

Step 3: Execution requests another five hundred megabytes for an aggregation. Storage is already at its protected baseline, so nothing more can be evicted, and the free space is insufficient. Spark would spill this operation's working data to disk.

Step 4: The demo logs each step so the borrowing-then-eviction sequence and the final spill are visible, illustrating that execution reclaims from storage but never below the protected baseline.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:24:00 INFO    Cache the accounts reference dataset (storage borrows idle space)
2026-10-30 05:24:00 INFO    Storage cached 700MB (storageUsed=700)
2026-10-30 05:24:00 INFO    Transactions join needs execution memory
2026-10-30 05:24:00 WARNING Execution evicted 200MB of cached storage (priority)
2026-10-30 05:24:00 INFO    Another aggregation needs still more execution memory
2026-10-30 05:24:00 SEVERE  Execution needs 500MB but only 0MB reclaimable → SPILL to disk
2026-10-30 05:24:00 INFO    Unified memory model demo complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark's unified memory model splits the heap region it manages for data processing into Execution Memory and Storage Memory. Execution Memory holds the transient working set of shuffles, joins, sorts, and aggregations, while Storage Memory holds cached and persisted partitions. The size of the managed region is set by spark.memory.fraction, around sixty percent of usable heap by default, with the rest left as user memory, and within that region spark.memory.storageFraction sets a protected baseline for storage, around half by default. The crucial feature is that the boundary between the two is dynamic rather than a fixed wall.

The borrowing is mutual but the priority is asymmetric. If storage is idle, execution can use the whole region for its shuffles and joins, and if execution is idle, storage can expand for caching. But execution has priority: when it needs space it can evict cached blocks that storage borrowed beyond its protected baseline, because an evicted cached partition can simply be recomputed or re-read, whereas interrupting an active sort or hash table would fail the computation. Storage can never forcibly reclaim memory that execution is actively using. If execution still cannot get enough even after reclaiming from storage, it spills to disk.

At the National Bank of India this mattered constantly. A job that cached a reference accounts dataset and then ran a heavy transactions join would see execution evict the borrowed cache when the join needed memory, which was fine because the cache could be rebuilt, but a job that over-cached would push execution into spilling and run slowly. The non-obvious lesson I share in interviews is that the symptom of too much caching is not a cache error but slow shuffles from spilling, so when diagnosing memory pressure I look at the storage tab and the spill metrics in the Spark UI together, unpersist aggressively, and avoid caching data used only once. The unified model replaced the old static split precisely so that an idle region never goes to waste, and understanding the execution-over-storage priority is what lets you reason about why a job spills.
